title: Stocks vs Alternatives: Understanding the Trade-offs
subtitle: How equities, REITs, InvITs, and bonds differ in risk, cash flow, and growth
summary: Comparing equity shares with REITs, InvITs, and debt bonds to understand how varying asset classes serve different financial goals like capital growth versus regular income.

sources.name: SEBI Investor Education and Protection Fund

disclaimer: Educational information only. Not investment advice. TradeOne is not a SEBI-registered investment adviser. Rules, taxes and yields change; verify with official sources.

sections.title: Why Compare Stocks with Other Asset Classes?
sections.content: Most retail investors start with common equity shares (stocks). When you buy a share, you are an owner of the company's future profits. While equities offer the highest historical potential for long-term compounding, they also experience the sharpest market drawdowns and provide unpredictable dividend cash flows. Alternatives like REITs, InvITs, and bonds offer contrasting characteristics: contractual cash flows, regulated payouts, or sovereign capital guarantees.
sections.analogy: Think of an equity stock like planting a fruit tree: it can grow tall over many years, but bad weather can delay harvests. A bond is like a water contract delivering a measured bucket of water every Monday. A REIT is like owning a rented shop in a bustling bazaar.

sections.title: Comparing Core Return Drivers
sections.content: Where returns originate across asset classes:
points: Stocks: Driven predominantly by business earnings growth, market multiple expansion, and discretionary dividends.
REITs: Driven primarily by contractual corporate office rent, high 90% payout mandates, and modest real estate value growth.
InvITs: Driven by utility toll and power grid tariffs with scheduled capital amortizations over concession lifespans.
Government & Corporate Bonds: Driven by predetermined contractual coupon rates and contractual maturity par value (subject to credit health).

sections.title: Risk and Volatility Spectrum
points: Equity Volatility: High (annual price fluctuations can easily exceed 20-40% during bear cycles).
REIT/InvIT Volatility: Moderate (units trade on stock exchanges and fluctuate with interest rates, but high cash yields provide a valuation cushion).
Bond Volatility: Lower (bond prices move with interest rate shifts, but holding to maturity returns par value).

sections.title: Balancing Asset Classes in a Portfolio
sections.content: Many retail portfolios in India are 100% concentrated in single equities, leaving them vulnerable during extended market corrections. Looking at alternatives allows investors to pair growth assets (stocks) with income-generating assets (REITs/InvITs) and capital preservation assets (G-Secs/Bonds).

sections.title: Worked Example: The Compounding vs Cash Flow Trade-off
sections.content: Suppose an investor holds ₹10,00,000 across two theoretical allocations:
details: Portfolio 1 (100% Equity): At 1.2% dividend yield, annual cash payout is ₹12,000. Capital fluctuations are wider.

Portfolio 2 (60% Equity, 20% REIT/InvIT, 20% Bonds): At an average income yield of approx. 4.2% across the blended basket, annual cash payout is ₹42,000, creating predictable quarterly and semi-annual cash inflows.
Trade-off: Portfolio 1 has higher theoretical long-term growth potential; Portfolio 2 provides immediate cash flow resilience and lower drawdowns.

sections.title: Comparative Tax Snapshot
sections.content: Key tax rules under Finance Act 2024:
points: Listed Equities & Equity Mutual Funds: LTCG 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh (holding > 12 months); STCG 20% (holding <= 12 months).
Listed Units (REIT/InvIT): Same capital gains timeline (12.5% LTCG / 20% STCG). Cash payouts split into interest/dividend/capital repayment.
Listed Bonds (G-Secs & Corporate): Interest taxed at investor slab rate; LTCG 12.5% if held > 12 months.

items.myth: Bonds and REITs always deliver lower returns than stocks.
items.fact: Over multi-year flat or sideways equity markets, high-yielding REITs, InvITs, and bonds have historically outperformed equities on a total return basis.

items.myth: You need different demat accounts for stocks and bonds.
items.fact: A single NSDL or CDSL Demat account can hold equity shares, government bonds, corporate debentures, mutual funds, and REIT units simultaneously.

terms.definition: The practice of dividing an investment portfolio among different asset categories (stocks, bonds, real estate, cash).
